research.subject: The steamship Vanderbilt gave away: on March 17, 1862, Cornelius Vanderbilt met Abraham Lincoln about countering a Confederate ironclad. Asked his price, he offered his steamship as a gift. A 30-second film can focus on that reversal, with the subsequent congressional gold medal as an end-card payoff. The facts below distinguish the documented gift from proposed ship modifications that were not carried out.

looks.thing: Cornelius Vanderbilt — age and physical appearance
looks.look: He was 67 on March 17, 1862, calculated from his birth date of May 27, 1794. Vanderbilt University's account describes him as six feet tall, sinewy, with ruddy cheeks, a strong nose, square jaw, high forehead, and thick gray hair that eventually became white. These are general biographical descriptions, not a record of his appearance that particular morning. ([news.vanderbilt.edu](https://news.vanderbilt.edu/2011/04/11/the-commodores-civil-war/?utm_source=openai))

The Smithsonian's description of Nathaniel Jocelyn's 1846 portrait specifies a dark jacket and tie with a white shirt. This is a documented earlier wardrobe reference, not proof of what Vanderbilt wore to the 1862 meeting. The catalog title contains an erroneous death year; the useful evidence here is its description of the portrait. ([si.edu](https://www.si.edu/object/cornelius-vanderbilt-1794-1887-painting%3Asiris_ari_371102?utm_source=openai))

looks.thing: Abraham Lincoln — age, appearance and clothing limits
looks.look: Lincoln was 53, calculated from his February 12, 1809 birth date, and stood six feet four inches tall. A Smithsonian photograph documents his beard in 1861. The Smithsonian's verbal description of a February 1865 portrait identifies sunken cheeks, a bushy beard, and a dark jacket with wide lapels over a matching vest. The latter is a later reference, not documentation of his March 1862 clothing. ([home.nps.gov](https://home.nps.gov/liho/learn/historyculture/lincolnfacts.htm?utm_source=openai))

looks.thing: Secretary of War Edwin M. Stanton
looks.look: Stanton was 47, calculated from his December 19, 1814 birth date. The university account describes rounded shoulders, receding hair slicked back, small round spectacles, and a gray beard without a moustache. Its stated age of 46 is inconsistent with the NPS birth date. His meeting-day clothing is not established by these sources. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/people/edwin-m-stanton.htm?ms=nav&utm_source=openai))

looks.thing: White House, Washington, D.C. — meeting location
looks.look: The NPS identifies Georgian and neoclassical influences in James Hoban's design. The meeting account establishes the White House but does not identify a particular room or furnishings; do not present an invented room arrangement as verified. No modern West Wing should appear: it was a later addition. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/places/white-house.htm?utm_source=openai))

A former transatlantic passenger-and-mail steamer, classified by the Navy as a side-wheel steamer. The university account specifies enormous side paddlewheels and two smokestacks. NHHC image NH 60881 supplies an identified artwork reference. These textual descriptions do not establish her precise March 1862 sail rig or paint colors; those details should not be invented. ([history.navy.mil](https://www.history.navy.mil/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/v/vanderbilt.html?utm_source=openai))

looks.thing: CSS Virginia — threatened opponent, if shown
looks.look: A casemate ironclad ram converted from the burned USS Merrimack. NHHC provides the identified visual reference NH 58881. Use the original Virginia, not the later Virginia II, and do not substitute a turreted Monitor-type vessel. ([history.navy.mil](https://www.history.navy.mil/content/history/nhhc/browse-by-topic/wars-conflicts-and-operations/civil-war/cw-operations-and-engagements/1862-civil-war/hampton-roads.html?utm_source=openai))

The documented proposal specified concrete inside the bow and reinforcing iron plating. The Navy explicitly says this modification was not carried out. It may be described as an idea, but should not be shown as completed historical work. No verified drawing or dimensions are supplied here. ([history.navy.mil](https://www.history.navy.mil/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/v/vanderbilt.html?utm_source=openai))

looks.thing: Congressional gold medal — optional closing image
looks.look: The university catalog describes Vanderbilt's profile on one side with the inscription 'A Grateful Country to her Generous Son.' The reverse has standing and kneeling figures, an eagle, a ship, and a Latin inscription. It credits Salathiel Ellis and Emmanuel Leutze as designers. This is a later acknowledgment, not an object present at the March 1862 meeting. ([collections.library.vanderbilt.edu](https://collections.library.vanderbilt.edu/repositories/2/archival_objects/656328?utm_source=openai))

facts.fact: The immediate problem was CSS Virginia: its March 8 attack on Union ships at Hampton Roads, followed by its March 9 fight with USS Monitor, created the crisis behind Vanderbilt's offer. ([history.navy.mil](https://www.history.navy.mil/content/history/nhhc/browse-by-topic/wars-conflicts-and-operations/civil-war/cw-operations-and-engagements/1862-civil-war/hampton-roads.html?utm_source=openai))

Secretary of War Edwin Stanton escorted Cornelius Vanderbilt to meet President Abraham Lincoln at the White House in Washington, D.C. ([news.vanderbilt.edu](https://news.vanderbilt.edu/2011/04/11/the-commodores-civil-war/))

Vanderbilt believed his large steamship Vanderbilt could destroy Virginia by collision. Lincoln asked how much he would charge for the vessel's services. ([news.vanderbilt.edu](https://news.vanderbilt.edu/2011/04/11/the-commodores-civil-war/))

Instead of naming a price, Vanderbilt offered to donate the ship, conditional on controlling its preparations for battle. This is the episode's factual dramatic reversal; reconstructed dialogue should not be passed off as a verbatim transcript. ([news.vanderbilt.edu](https://news.vanderbilt.edu/2011/04/11/the-commodores-civil-war/))

Vanderbilt proposed filling the bow with concrete and reinforcing it with iron plating for use against Virginia. The Navy's history explicitly states that this particular modification was not performed. ([history.navy.mil](https://www.history.navy.mil/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/v/vanderbilt.html?utm_source=openai))
facts.when: Early 1862; precise proposal date not specified

facts.fact: The ship was transferred to the Navy on March 24. During summer 1862, the New York Navy Yard fitted her with a battery of fifteen guns. ([history.navy.mil](https://www.history.navy.mil/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/v/vanderbilt.html?utm_source=openai))

In a formal message to Congress, Lincoln confirmed that Vanderbilt had given the ocean steamer to the United States without payment in March, and recommended an appropriate acknowledgment. This is primary-source confirmation of the gift. ([govinfo.gov](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/SERIALSET-01123_00_00-007-0071-0000/pdf/SERIALSET-01123_00_00-007-0071-0000.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Congress subsequently honored Vanderbilt with a gold medal in appreciation of his gift of the steamship to the Union Navy—a documented closing payoff for the film. ([collections.library.vanderbilt.edu](https://collections.library.vanderbilt.edu/repositories/2/archival_objects/656328?utm_source=openai))

story.style: Live-action, period-accurate documentary realism; restrained close-ups and static framing; naturalistic light.
story.story:
An opening caption establishes the crisis: on March 8, 1862, CSS Virginia attacked Union ships at Hampton Roads; on March 9, it fought USS Monitor. These events prompted Cornelius Vanderbilt’s offer.

March 17, 1862. At the White House in Washington, D.C., Secretary of War Edwin Stanton escorts Cornelius Vanderbilt to meet President Abraham Lincoln.

A cutaway shows the large steamship Vanderbilt. Narration explains Vanderbilt’s belief that his vessel could destroy CSS Virginia by collision. Back at the meeting, narration conveys Lincoln’s question about how much Vanderbilt would charge for the vessel’s services.

The camera holds on Cornelius Vanderbilt as narration reveals his answer: instead of naming a price, he offers to donate the ship to the United States, provided he controls its preparations for battle.
story.title: Instead of a Price
